# Checking whether the line deserves your trust {#sec-linear-regression-assumptions}

















We ended the last chapter admitting something uncomfortable out loud: the line in @fig-what_intercept_slope, drawn straight across every DPI from 0 to 30, is almost certainly the wrong model for how tissue area behaves after ischemia. We said we would come back to that. This is us coming back to it.

Here's the part your computer will never tell you: `lm()` and `brm()` don't check whether a straight line makes sense for your data before fitting one. They fit it, coefficients and all, whether or not the result means anything. Five assumptions decide whether those coefficients are worth trusting: linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, normality of the residuals, and no multicollinearity. None of them is checked automatically. That job is yours, and it's the whole subject of this chapter.

::: callout-warning
Neither R, `brms`, SPSS, nor STATA will pop up a warning window telling you your assumptions are violated. Verifying them is a modeling step, not an afterthought, as much a part of "fitting a model" as writing the formula.
:::

::: callout-tip
## The five assumptions we'll check

- Linearity
- Independence
- Homoscedasticity
- Normality of residuals
- No multicollinearity
:::

## Linearity

Think about your own weight over your lifetime. From birth through childhood, it climbs at a fairly steady clip: roughly one straight line, age in, weight out. Push that same line into adolescence, adulthood, and beyond, though, and it falls apart: diet, activity, metabolism, and a dozen other things start pulling weight around in ways age alone can't predict, and the trajectory plateaus, wobbles, sometimes reverses. The relationship didn't stop being real. It stopped being a *straight* one. That is [linearity]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} as an assumption, not as a definition: a linear regression doesn't ask "is $x$ related to $y$?" It assumes the specific shape of that relationship is a straight line, given by @eq-linear-regression-simple, and everything downstream (the coefficients, their uncertainty, any prediction you make from them) inherits that assumption whether it's true or not.

You've already watched this assumption look shaky, on real data, in the last chapter. @fig-what_intercept_slope fit one straight line across the full 0 to 30 DPI range of `cell_data`, and we flagged, without proving it, that this was probably the wrong call. Let's prove it. But first, one fact about who is in this dataset, because it changes how every plot below reads. @tbl-assumptions_dpi_summary lists each DPI group, the condition of the animals in it, and what tissue area looks like there.








::: {#tbl-assumptions_dpi_summary .cell tbl-cap='Who is in each DPI group, and tissue area (mm²) in each'}

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(all(tapply(cell_data$Condition, cell_data$DPI, function(x) length(unique(x))) == 1))

dpi_summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(cell_data, cell_data$DPI), function(g) {
  data.frame(
    DPI = g$DPI[1],
    Condition = as.character(g$Condition[1]),
    n = nrow(g),
    mean_area = mean(g$Tissue_Area),
    sd_area = sd(g$Tissue_Area)
  )
}))

gt(dpi_summary) |>
  cols_label(DPI = "DPI", Condition = "Condition", n = "n", mean_area = "Mean (mm²)", sd_area = "SD (mm²)") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(mean_area, sd_area), decimals = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
\begin{table}
\fontsize{12.0pt}{14.4pt}\selectfont
\begin{tabular*}{\linewidth}{@{\extracolsep{\fill}}rlrrr}
\toprule
DPI & Condition & n & Mean (mm²) & SD (mm²) \\ 
\midrule\addlinespace[2.5pt]
0 & SHAM & 7 & 14.57 & 0.68 \\ 
3 & MCAO & 8 & 16.90 & 3.10 \\ 
7 & MCAO & 11 & 13.94 & 1.06 \\ 
14 & MCAO & 12 & 9.45 & 1.04 \\ 
30 & MCAO & 11 & 7.97 & 1.19 \\ 
\bottomrule
\end{tabular*}
\end{table}

:::
:::








Notice who sits where. All 7 `SHAM` animals are at day 0, and every `MCAO` animal is at day 3 or later. So "day 0" here means sham surgery, not ischemic tissue at the moment of injury, and the intercept of any line through this file is a sham mean (14.6 mm²). It also means that the step from day 0 to day 3 mixes two things, time and being injured, that this file cannot pull apart. We meet this limit of the design again in @sec-linear-regression-multiple, where it decides which questions the data can answer.

Now the model. I use `lm()` for the residual checks because a residual is a residual whichever engine produced it, and with a flat prior the residuals of a `brms` fit are essentially the same ones (we check that later in this chapter). What matters is what we do with them. If a straight line were the right description, then at every day the line should be right on average, and whatever is left over, the [residuals]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} (our estimates of the error terms $\epsilon_i$ from the last chapter: the observed value minus the line's prediction), should scatter around zero without any pattern. Plotting the residuals instead of the raw data is useful precisely because it subtracts the line: the trend disappears, and what remains is the line's mistakes, laid out where the eye can see them.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linearity_model <- lm(Tissue_Area ~ DPI, data = cell_data)
```
:::










Here are the residuals by day. Triangles are sham animals, circles are `MCAO`, and each orange diamond is the mean residual of its day.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
resid_df <- data.frame(
  DPI = cell_data$DPI,
  Condition = cell_data$Condition,
  residual = residuals(linearity_model)
)

ggplot(resid_df, aes(x = DPI, y = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_jitter(aes(shape = Condition), width = 0.6, height = 0, color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 18, size = 5, color = "#D55E00") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(SHAM = 17, MCAO = 16)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 7, 14, 30)) +
  labs(x = "Days post-injury (DPI)", y = "Residual (mm²)") +
  Plot_theme
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Residuals from the straight line through tissue area, by day post-injury. Orange diamonds mark the mean residual of each day. If the line were right on average at every day, they would sit on the dashed line.](linear-regression-assumptions_files/figure-pdf/fig-assumptions_linearity_residuals-1.png){#fig-assumptions_linearity_residuals fig-alt='Scatter of residuals in mm² against days post-injury at 0, 3, 7, 14 and 30. The orange group means fall below zero at days 0 and 14 and above zero at days 3 and 30.'}
:::
:::








If the line were a good description, the orange diamonds would sit on the dashed line. They don't. The line overshoots day 0 (the shams sit 0.9 mm² below it) and day 14 (2.1 mm² below), and it undershoots day 3 (2.3 mm² above) and, by less, day 30. Read left to right, the mean residuals go down, up, up a little, down, up. That is not noise around a line. It is a shape the line has no way to produce.

Here is the biology I read into that shape, and I hold it loosely. Tissue area is higher at day 3 than in the shams (by about 2.3 mm²) and then falls, but not at a constant rate: about 0.64 mm² per day between days 7 and 14, and only about 0.09 mm² per day between days 14 and 30. An early bump followed by a decline that flattens is what I would expect from acute edema, tissue that swells before it degenerates, followed by atrophy that levels off. But the day-3 bump rests on eight animals with a standard deviation of 3.1 mm², compared with seven shams. That gap of 2.3 mm² has a standard error of about 1.1, and it compares different animals under different conditions. So "edema" is my reading of the shape, not something this dataset can prove. What the dataset does prove is the failure of linearity itself: the residuals have structure, and no straight line can follow a bump followed by a plateau.

::: callout-tip
Real biological relationships are under no obligation to be straight lines, and a line forced onto a curve doesn't just fit a little worse: it hands you a single slope for a process that, in different stretches of time, is doing different things. Knowing your system well enough to *expect* a shape like this before you plot it is what turns a diagnostic check into something more than guesswork.
:::

A tempting fix here, and one plenty of tutorials reach for immediately, is a log or square-root transform to force the curvature into a straight line. I'd rather not reach for that by default. Pablo Inchausti calls these "esoteric transformations" [@inchausti2023], and I agree with his objection: they often buy linearity at the cost of interpretability, leaving you with coefficients for "log tissue area" that no longer mean anything to a biologist. Better tools exist for exactly this (nonlinear and multilevel growth models, covered in @sec-longitudinal-timeseries), so a distorting transformation is rarely the best option available to you anymore.

## Independence

Picture a mouse run three times on a rotarod, with the time to fall recorded each time. Those three numbers are not three independent draws; they are one mouse's motor learning curve sampled three times, and treating them as independent observations quietly triples your apparent sample size without earning it. That is the intuition behind [independence]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}: each observation should bring its own information, not echo a neighbor. Formally, the error terms $\epsilon_i$ must be uncorrelated across observations.

Dependence comes in two flavors worth keeping apart. The rotarod is a case of clustering: rows that share an animal resemble each other more than rows from different animals. The other flavor is serial: values taken close together in time resemble each other, as with a reading logged every minute. Clustering is the one you will meet most often at the bench. Serial dependence is easier to see on a page, so that's the one the figure below draws.

Is `cell_data` at risk? Not here, and by design: it has 49 rows and 49 different `MouseID`s, one row per animal, so no two rows share a mouse. That is what lets this whole part treat every row as an independent observation. The moment you go below the animal level, with several sections per animal or several cells per section, rows start sharing an animal and the rotarod problem is back. Fixing that is the job of @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts, once you have the machinery it needs. For now, a small simulation makes the failure visible without it.

<!-- TODO(real data): replace this simulated series, and the paragraph after the figure, with real clustered data (section-level rows with several rows per MouseID, or repeated rotarod sessions), once Daniel provides the dataset. Review of 2026-10-02. -->








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(8807)
time_steps <- seq(1, 100, by = 1)

response_independent <- 5 + 0.3 * time_steps + rnorm(100, mean = 0, sd = 5)

response_dependent <- numeric(100)
response_dependent[1] <- 5 + rnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = 5)
for (i in 2:100) {
  response_dependent[i] <- 5 + 0.3 * time_steps[i] +
    0.8 * response_dependent[i - 1] + rnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = 5)
}

data_independence <- rbind(
  data.frame(time = time_steps, response = response_independent, type = "Independent"),
  data.frame(time = time_steps, response = response_dependent, type = "Dependent (autocorrelated)")
)

ggplot(data_independence, aes(x = time, y = response)) +
  geom_line(color = "#0072B2") +
  facet_wrap(~type) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Response") +
  Plot_theme
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Independent vs. autocorrelated observations over time](linear-regression-assumptions_files/figure-pdf/fig-assumptions_independence-1.png){#fig-assumptions_independence}
:::
:::








Both panels use the same recipe for the noise, but in the second each value also inherits 80% of the one before it, which makes it drift upward much more steeply than the first. Ignore the slope and look at the texture. The independent panel is jagged. The dependent one wanders like a trajectory, because each point mostly repeats its neighbor. A model that treats those 100 points as 100 independent pieces of evidence is counting the same information many times over, and its intervals will be narrower than the evidence deserves. This is not a rare mistake: repeated measures from the same animal, subject, or preparation get treated as independent observations often enough that it's worth naming as its own failure mode, separate from "wrong shape" or "wrong variance."

## Homoscedasticity

Think of a bench balance. Weigh something light and it is good to a milligram; weigh something near its capacity and it wobbles by a few hundred. You would never write "balance error: plus or minus half a milligram" on the label and be done, because the honest margin depends on what you are weighing. A linear model, by default, writes exactly that label: one leftover spread, $\sigma$, for every animal at every day. [Homoscedasticity]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} is the assumption that this single number is honest, that the spread of the residuals is the same wherever you look along the predictor. Its opposite, [heteroscedasticity]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}, is a balance that wobbles more as the load grows.

What breaks when it fails is the margin the model reports. One $\sigma$ for all days means that predictions of where a new animal would land are too narrow where the real spread is large and too wide where it is small. The standard error of the slope also rests on that single $\sigma$, and it can end up too small or too large depending on where the spread sits relative to the design. <!-- TODO(Daniel/NotebookLM Q3): cite a textbook for the consequences of unequal variance (coefficient standard errors vs. prediction intervals). --> So this is worth checking, and the residuals we already have let us do it. Here they are again, this time for two outcomes from the same animals: tissue area, and GFAP integrated density, the marker whose spread we eyeballed back in the exploration part. Each bar is the mean of a day's residuals plus and minus one standard deviation, so the length of the bar is the spread.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
gfap_model <- lm(Gfap_IntDen ~ DPI, data = cell_data)

spread_df <- rbind(
  data.frame(outcome = "Tissue area (mm²)", DPI_f = cell_data$DPI_f, Condition = cell_data$Condition,
             residual = residuals(linearity_model)),
  data.frame(outcome = "GFAP integrated density", DPI_f = cell_data$DPI_f, Condition = cell_data$Condition,
             residual = residuals(gfap_model))
)

spread_df$outcome <- factor(spread_df$outcome, levels = c("Tissue area (mm²)", "GFAP integrated density"))

mean_pm_sd <- function(x) data.frame(y = mean(x), ymin = mean(x) - sd(x), ymax = mean(x) + sd(x))

ggplot(spread_df, aes(x = DPI_f, y = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_jitter(aes(shape = Condition), width = 0.15, height = 0, color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_pm_sd, geom = "pointrange", color = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.9, size = 0.8) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(SHAM = 17, MCAO = 16)) +
  facet_wrap(~outcome, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Days post-injury (DPI)", y = "Residual") +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 14))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Residual spread by DPI for two straight-line fits, one for tissue area and one for GFAP integrated density. Orange bars show the mean residual of each day plus and minus one standard deviation.](linear-regression-assumptions_files/figure-pdf/fig-assumptions_homoscedasticity-1.png){#fig-assumptions_homoscedasticity fig-alt='Two panels of residuals against days post-injury. In the tissue area panel the day 3 residuals are much more spread out than at other days. In the GFAP panel the spread is tiny at day 0 and grows by about tenfold from day 7 onward.'}
:::
:::










In the left panel, the spread of tissue area is about 0.7 mm² at day 0, between 1 and 1.2 mm² at days 7, 14 and 30, and 3.1 mm² at day 3: roughly three times wider than its neighbors. In the right panel, GFAP is the textbook case: the spread grows from about 25 at day 0 to 71 at day 3 and to between 247 and 319 from day 7 on, a tenfold change. That is the trumpet from @fig-eda-ggplot-trumpet, now measured on a model's residuals instead of eyeballed. Tissue area misbehaves differently, with one unusually wide day instead of a steady widening. Two outcomes from the same animals, two different ways of breaking the same assumption.

For GFAP, the story I told in the exploration part still holds: a system that is stable at baseline and that diverges between animals as injury, degeneration and repair play out. For tissue area, a wide day 3 fits the idea that the first days are when animals differ most in how much their tissue swells, but as before, that is a reading, and it rests on eight animals.

Rather than reach for a log transform to flatten this spread, the more direct answer is to let the model's spread itself depend on the predictor, a distributional model, which we build properly in @sec-multivariate-distributional-regression. We meet the day-3 spread again, left open on purpose, in @sec-linear-regression-multiple. The short version worth holding onto: heteroscedasticity is not a defect to transform away. It is information about where your data are more and less trustworthy, and a model that can say so is more honest than one that cannot.

## Normality of residuals

The [normality]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} assumption is narrower than it sounds, and it's worth being precise about what it does and doesn't cover: it is a statement about the *residuals* (the leftover error), not about the predictors, and not about the raw response variable itself.

::: callout-warning
Normality applies to the model's residuals, not to the predictors or the response. A skewed response can still produce nicely normal residuals once the model accounts for what's driving that skew, and, as you're about to see, residuals can look normal even when something else about the model is badly wrong.
:::

Here is a genuinely useful, slightly humbling thing to notice: the same `linearity_model` we just used to expose two separate problems (a curve it can't follow, and a spread that isn't constant for either outcome) still produces residuals that look, well, fine. I draw two views of them because each shows something the other hides. The histogram gives you the shape at a glance and makes an outlier hard to miss. The Q-Q plot lines up the sorted residuals against the values a perfectly normal sample would give, so a normal sample hugs the diagonal, and the tails, which matter most for predictions, get stretched out where you can inspect them.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
res_df <- data.frame(residual = residuals(linearity_model))

p_hist <- ggplot(res_df, aes(x = residual)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 12, fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.8, color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Residual (mm²)", y = "Count") +
  Plot_theme

p_qq <- ggplot(res_df, aes(sample = residual)) +
  stat_qq(color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_qq_line(color = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Sample quantiles (mm²)") +
  Plot_theme

p_hist + p_qq + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Histogram (A) and Q-Q plot (B) of the residuals from the straight line through tissue area](linear-regression-assumptions_files/figure-pdf/fig-assumptions_normality-1.png){#fig-assumptions_normality fig-alt='A roughly bell-shaped histogram of residuals in mm² next to a Q-Q plot whose points follow the diagonal line closely, with small departures at both ends.'}
:::
:::










Both panels look about as a normal sample should: roughly bell-shaped, close to the diagonal, with a few points wandering at the ends, as 49 points will. A Shapiro-Wilk test says the same (W = 0.97, p = 0.36), but I include it mostly to show how little a test adds here: with 49 animals it has little power to detect anything, so failing to reject normality is not evidence for it. And yet we know this model is misspecified: we just spent two sections showing that its linearity and homoscedasticity assumptions both fail. That is the point worth sitting with. Normality checks one specific thing, and it has nothing useful to say about whether the *shape* of your model is right. A residual histogram that looks like a perfect bell curve is not a clean bill of health; it is one assumption cleared out of five, no more and no less.

So why doesn't this book spend more time on residual normality? Because $\hat{\beta}_0$ and $\hat{\beta}_1$ are themselves weighted averages of the data, and a weighted average of enough observations tends toward a normal sampling distribution by the central limit theorem, regardless of how the individual residuals are shaped: skewed, bimodal, whatever. That's why Gelman, Hill, and Vehtari are comfortable saying, bluntly, that "for the purpose of estimating the regression line (as compared to predicting individual data points), the assumption of normality is typically barely important at all," and they do not recommend diagnostics of residual normality at all [@gelman2020]. Inchausti treats minor departures from normality as tolerable once your sample size is reasonable [@inchausti2023]. I still draw the two plots once, for a reason that is about prediction rather than about the line: the one place this protection genuinely runs out is when your goal shifts from estimating the line to predicting where one *new*, individual animal will land. An individual prediction interval depends on the actual shape of the residual tail, not just the mean, and no amount of sample size fixes that if the tail is badly behaved.

![Two ways to meet a model that doesn't quite fit: stretch one off-the-rack garment over every body, or tailor one to the shape in front of you.](images/model_fit.png){#fig-fitmodels fig-align="center" width="60%" fig-alt="Black and white ink sketch of the same woman twice. On the left she holds up a shapeless, oversized gown that balloons around her. On the right she wears a tailored dress with a fitted bodice and a flared skirt, hands on her hips."}

There are, broadly, two ways to respond to a model that doesn't quite fit, as @fig-fitmodels suggests. One is the ritualistic option: keep using the same linear regression regardless of what the data actually look like, and stretch its robustness as far as it will go. The other is to become the kind of modeling tailor who reaches for the tool built for the shape of the data in front of them: nonlinear terms, varying variance, whatever the biology actually calls for. Over the next few chapters, you'll have an entire wardrobe to choose from. There's rarely a good reason to keep reaching for the one ill-fitting suit.

For outcomes where normal residuals genuinely aren't realistic to expect (reaction times with a long right tail, for instance), @sec-beta-robust-regression covers robust alternatives like Student-t regression directly, rather than asking you to force normality onto data that was never going to give it to you.

## Reading the same assumptions as a Bayesian

There is another way to ask whether a model describes your data, and you met it in @sec-mcmc-model-checking: let the fitted model write fake datasets and lay them next to the real one. If the model is a good description, its fakes should look like your data. If the real data stick out somewhere the fakes never go, an assumption is failing in the open. It is the same detective work as a residual plot, except that instead of one leftover per animal you compare whole replicated datasets, one for every posterior draw.

I fit the same full-range line with `brms`. As in @sec-intro-applied-modeling, I leave the default priors on purpose: the point here is the check, not the prior (@sec-priors-regularization is where priors get chosen deliberately), and with 49 animals and a diffuse prior the likelihood does nearly all the work.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(brms)
library(posterior)

assumptions_fit <- brm(
  Tissue_Area ~ DPI,
  data = cell_data,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/linear-regression-assumptions_fit1.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```
:::










The fit passes the three sampler checks from @sec-mcmc-model-checking: the largest Rhat is 1.001, the smallest bulk and tail effective sample sizes are 3657 and 2946, and there are 0 divergent transitions. Now the check itself. A residual plot looked at the mean residual of each day and at its spread. The posterior predictive version asks the same two questions of the model directly: if the fitted line were the true process, what mean and what spread would we expect to see on each day, and are the real ones among them? That is `pp_check()` with `type = "stat_grouped"`, once for the mean (the linearity question) and once for the standard deviation (the spread question).








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(123)

day_label <- as_labeller(function(x) paste("Day", x))
no_counts <- theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 12), axis.text.y = element_blank(),
                   axis.ticks.y = element_blank(), axis.line.y = element_blank())

p_mean <- pp_check(assumptions_fit, type = "stat_grouped", stat = "mean", group = "DPI", ndraws = 1000) +
  facet_wrap(~group, scales = "free", labeller = day_label) +
  labs(x = "Mean tissue area (mm²)") +
  Plot_theme + no_counts

p_sd <- pp_check(assumptions_fit, type = "stat_grouped", stat = "sd", group = "DPI", ndraws = 1000) +
  facet_wrap(~group, scales = "free", labeller = day_label) +
  labs(x = "SD of tissue area (mm²)") +
  Plot_theme + no_counts + theme(legend.position = "none")

p_mean / p_sd + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Posterior predictive checks by day. Pale bars are the distribution of the statistic across 1,000 replicated datasets from the fitted straight line, and the dark line is the real value. Panel A uses the mean (linearity), panel B the standard deviation (spread).](linear-regression-assumptions_files/figure-pdf/fig-assumptions_ppc-1.png){#fig-assumptions_ppc fig-alt='Two rows of small histograms, one per day post-injury. In the top row, the observed mean falls in the far right tail at day 3 and in the far left tail at day 14. In the bottom row, the observed standard deviation falls in the far left tail at days 0, 7, 14 and 30.'}
:::
:::










Panel A is the linearity story told again. Days 0, 7 and 30 sit comfortably inside their clouds, but day 3 and day 14 do not: only 0.5% of the replicated day-3 means were as large as the real one, and 99.8% of the replicated day-14 means were larger than the real one. A straight line that is right on average at three days out of five and badly off at the other two is not a line I would summarize this experiment with.

Panel B is where the Bayesian lens adds something the residual plot didn't say in so many words. The model has a single $\sigma$ (about 2.2 mm²), so it expects every day to be about equally variable. The real animals are much more tightly packed than that on four of five days: for day 0, 99.6% of replicated datasets had a larger spread than the real shams. The one day that is more variable than the model expects, day 3, is only moderately surprising on its own (7.0% of replicated spreads were as large as the real one). The cleaner way to say what the residual plots showed is that one $\sigma$ is too big for four days and somewhat too small for one, because it is averaging over all of them.

@sec-mcmc-model-checking made the point that a failed check is not an automatic verdict: whether a failure matters depends on what you want from the model. For the GFAP model there, a few impossible negative predictions did not matter for the target, a difference between group means. Here the target would be a single rate of tissue change over thirty days, and the checks say the line is wrong on average at two of five time points. That one I would not report.

::: callout-tip
### Frequentist equivalent

The residual plots in the sections before this one are the frequentist version of these checks, and the two fits agree on the line itself: the intercept is 15.46 mm² in `lm()` and 15.47 in `brms`, the slope -0.277 and -0.277 mm² per day. As in @sec-intro-applied-modeling, a diffuse prior lets the likelihood do the work, so the agreement is expected. The two lenses would only start to disagree with small samples or with priors that say something. What differs is the check, not the line: residuals ask what is left over for each animal, while posterior predictive checks ask whether the model could have produced data like ours.
:::

## No multicollinearity

Imagine reading the temperature of one beaker with two thermometers, one in Celsius and one in Fahrenheit, and asking what temperature does to enzyme activity. The model has to split the credit between two instruments that say exactly the same thing, and it can't: any weight it takes from one it can hand to the other without changing a single prediction, so the individual coefficients become unstable even though the fit itself is fine. That is [multicollinearity]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}: predictors correlated strongly enough that they carry largely redundant information about the response. It only comes up once you have two or more predictors.

<!-- TODO(Daniel/NotebookLM Q1): confirm how Gelman, Hill & Vehtari (and others) treat collinearity: part of the list of assumptions, or a separate issue of precision and interpretation. Adjust this section's framing, and the "five assumptions" wording in the opening, accordingly. -->

You've already done the legwork for this one, back in @sec-eda-ggpairs: a pairwise correlation matrix on this dataset showed `Pdgfrb_Area` and `Pdgfrb_IntDen`, and `Gfap_Area` and `Gfap_IntDen`, each strongly correlated (Pearson's $r$ of 0.94 and 0.99, respectively). Each pair is a pair of thermometers: two measurements of the same underlying signal. That was a general finding, made before any model was on the table. With an actual regression model in front of us, the question sharpens from "are these correlated?" to "how much is that correlation distorting *this* model's coefficients?" The [variance inflation factor]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} (VIF) answers exactly that. For a predictor $j$, you regress it on all the other predictors, take the $R_j^2$ of that regression (how well the others can already reproduce it), and compute:

$$
\text{VIF}_j = \frac{1}{1 - R_j^2}
$$ {#eq-vif}

A predictor the others can't reproduce at all has $R_j^2 = 0$ and a VIF of 1. As $R_j^2$ approaches 1, the VIF explodes. Its meaning is direct: the variance of that predictor's coefficient is VIF times larger than it would be if the predictor were unrelated to the others, so its standard error is $\sqrt{\text{VIF}}$ times larger. I keep only the columns involved, so the model call is easy to read, and fit a model for tissue area with one PDGFR-β and both GFAP predictors.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(car)

cell_data_sub <- subset(cell_data, select = c(Tissue_Area, Pdgfrb_Area, Pdgfrb_IntDen, Gfap_Area, Gfap_IntDen))

model <- lm(Tissue_Area ~ Pdgfrb_Area + Gfap_Area + Gfap_IntDen, data = cell_data_sub)

vif_values <- vif(model)
vif_values
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Pdgfrb_Area   Gfap_Area Gfap_IntDen 
    1.74181    47.37687    50.03761 
```


:::
:::








`Gfap_Area` and `Gfap_IntDen` carry VIFs of about 47 and 50, against 1.7 for `Pdgfrb_Area` [@car]. A VIF of 50 means a standard error about 7.1 times larger than it would otherwise be. A common rule of thumb flags a VIF above 5, and above 10 as serious. <!-- TODO(Daniel/NotebookLM Q2): cite a textbook source for the VIF 5 / 10 rule of thumb. --> This is not a subtle warning: it is the two GFAP predictors actively fighting each other for credit over the same underlying signal.

The most direct fix is simply to drop one. Including both `Gfap_Area` and `Gfap_IntDen` adds no real information the model didn't already have from the other, while inflating standard errors and destabilizing both coefficients. Which one to drop is a judgment call, not a statistical one: weigh which is easier to measure reliably, which is more interpretable for your specific question, and which better matches the biological quantity you actually care about. (If you ever find yourself choosing between age and a genuine preference for pistachio gelato as competing predictors, go with age; it generalizes better across studies.) Feature engineering [@kuhn2021], building a new composite variable from the correlated pair instead of just discarding one, is the other real option, and one we'll return to once multiple-predictor models are the norm rather than the exception.

::: callout-tip
When multicollinearity forces a choice, favor the predictor that's easier to measure reliably and more directly tied to the biological question, not just whichever has the smaller VIF.
:::

## Where this leaves us

Five assumptions, and what they said about one straight line across the full DPI range of `cell_data`. Linearity fails: the line is clearly wrong on average at two of five days, in a shape (a bump, then a decline that flattens) that no straight line can follow, in a dataset where "day 0" is a different group of animals, not the same animals at an earlier time. The spread is not constant, and it breaks that assumption in two different ways for two outcomes: one wide day for tissue area, a steady widening for GFAP. Normality looks fine, which is exactly why it can't be the only thing you check. Independence holds by design in this file, because each row is a different animal, and stops holding the moment you go below the animal level. And collinearity is a problem as soon as both GFAP measures share a model. That's the real lesson of this chapter, more than any one assumption on its own: these checks aren't independent boxes to tick, and passing one tells you nothing about the others. The Bayesian and frequentist versions of the checks tell the same story, because they are asking the same questions of the same line.

None of this means the line from @fig-what_intercept_slope was a wasted exercise, and it doesn't mean linear regression is the wrong tool for this dataset. It means the *full* 0 to 30 DPI range was the wrong range to ask it to cover in one go. @sec-linear-regression-single-continuous picks this exact problem back up, does the one thing this chapter's diagnostics recommend (restrict the range to where a straight line is a defensible description of the biology) and, unlike this chapter, takes it all the way through to a fitted, interpreted, `brms`-and-`parsnip` model with something to say about the effect of time on tissue area.
